title: About Dainyel
text: Meet the Dutch travel creator behind Dainyel on the Move. My story, travel style and the experiences that keep me curious.
keywords: Home About Dainyel Dainyel on the move The person behind the journey. Personal stories, curiosity and a camera on the road. Share this page → From Emmen, the Netherlands · travelling since 18 One trip opened the door. My friends and family have always known me as the one ready for the next trip. DainyelOnTheMove simply gave that feeling a name. At 18, I went to Barcelona with someone who quickly became one of my closest friends. That first shared adventure made travel feel like more than a holiday and started an appetite for seeing much more of the world. What keeps me travelling is the people, cultures and perspectives I find along the way: a local meal, a good night out, an early hike or somewhere I did not expect to find. Travel is not a scorecard. It is the perspective you bring home, and the respect you show while you are away. A little background Home base Emmen, Drenthe, the Netherlands International Business Bachelor’s degree and practical projects across Europe and Asia Study exchange Three months in Thailand and three months in Bali The person behind the passport Beyond the highlight reel. A little more about me and the way I travel. Open whichever part you are curious about. People & local life I am social, adventurous and open-minded. I like seeing a culture through the eyes of the people who live there: listening first, trying the food and respecting local norms. Working as an assistant manager taught me to read people, bring humour to a moment and make room for everyone. Hostels bring that same sense of connection to a trip; the shared stories often matter more than an extra hour of sleep. The rhythm of a trip I plan the essentials and leave room for detours. An early breakfast, exploring or taking it slow, a drink somewhere new, dinner and a night out: I like a little bit of everything. I am an animal lover and try to make time for an animal park or zoo when I travel. Nature, wildlife, hiking, snorkelling and diving help me slow down. A gym session, bike ride or hike keeps my mind clear, at home or away. “No importa el camino, lo importante es seguir caminando.” The path does not matter; what matters is that you keep walking. The gadget man My camera, travel tech and a bag full of practical things always come with me. Friends gave me the nickname “gadget-man”; it is how I make sure a moment does not disappear when the trip ends. title: Bali Travel Story: Three Months in Denpasar
text: An honest Bali travel blog about three months in Indonesia: study life in Denpasar, family adventures, local nights and island escapes.
keywords: Home Travel stories Bali Bali · Indonesia · 2024–2025 Bali: the famous influencer island… At least, that is what the socials suggest. My three months there held family memories, student life, island adventures, a local bar I practically adopted—and an honest view beyond the postcard. Words & images by Dainyel 2024–2025 3 months Event Management Approx. 6 min read Read at your own pace. Explore the chapters below. Bali & the nearby islands · 2024–2025 Study exchange · a personal story Beyond the picture-perfect feed. I went to Bali excited to explore it with my family, classmates and the people I met along the way. I came home with beautiful memories—and a more complicated opinion of the island than the polished clips online tend to show. At a glance Family, study life, island escapes and an unfiltered reflection. Explore this destination → · Small moments from the archive → In this story Student life Island days My local spot Beyond Bali Alas Kedaton bats The honest view Back to the opening ↑ On social media, Bali can look like the perfect backdrop for an influencer lifestyle—or a course someone is trying to sell. I used to joke that I had come to do exactly that. Not really. My parents and brother came to visit me in Thailand shortly before we flew together to Bali in November 2024. We had a week to enjoy the island as a family before my next study minor began. I stayed in Denpasar while studying Event Management at UNTRIM University . The campus was about a five-minute scooter ride away. Over the next three months, Bali became a place of shared routines, spontaneous plans and experiences I still talk about—with classmates, family and the people I met there. My base in Denpasar Getting around on two wheels. I rented a scooter for about €70 a month. I could have found a cheaper one, but I wanted a fun scooter to ride. It quickly became part of everyday life: a way to get around Denpasar, meet up and explore the island at my own pace. My parents spent their holiday travelling from place to place. Whenever our plans lined up, we found plenty of time to enjoy Bali together. On the move A scooter, a new neighbourhood, and room to explore. It was a small part of the exchange, but it made the island feel more within reach—and gave me a ride I was genuinely excited to hop on. Beaches, mornings and big nights Bali kept offering a different kind of day. Some days were for the beach at Sanur or a walk along Kuta’s promenade. Other days meant heading out to the Ubud Monkey Forest, seeing the rice terraces at Tegallalang, or hiking Mount Batur. Bali also had its late nights: I went out at the large beach clubs Finns and Atlas, then found myself making plans for another early start. One of the most surreal experiences was swimming with dolphins in Lovina and seeing bioluminescent algae after dark. It is hard to forget a night when the water itself seems to glow. A slower moment by the water Giving surfing a go When the beach day turns to sunset A closer look at a civet A place that became a ritual My favourite spot was not a beach club. About a five-minute walk from my hotel was a local place called Warunk WOW . Most of the students I knew had barely heard of it. That was part of the charm: it felt like a local hangout rather than another stop on a visitor’s checklist. During the day, I could stop by for coffee or lunch in its open internet-café space. Upstairs, a small club room—around 200 people—hosted local DJs or a band. It kept a 24/7 rhythm: daytime café, then a club upstairs every evening. I ended up there almost daily, got to know the staff and regulars, and became a familiar face. I might even have been a little iconic in that room—at least, that is how I remember it. My Bali regular From coffee stop to second home. The best part was the people. A familiar place, friendly faces and a local DJ or band made the nights feel personal. See Warunk WOW on Instagram ↗ A little further afield Some of the brightest blues were beyond Bali. During the break in my studies, my classmates and I made trips to the islands around Bali: Nusa Lembongan, Nusa Ceningan, Nusa Penida, Lombok and the Gili Islands. We celebrated New Year’s Eve at Mad Monkey, a well-known party hostel on the Gilis. The beaches and coastlines on these nearby islands were genuinely beautiful. They gave us a welcome change of scenery from our everyday routine in Bali and made the holiday trips with my classmates even more memorable. A change of scenery with the group Cliffs above the sea A coastline worth lingering over One more evening by the water A moment in motion The flying foxes of Alas Kedaton. This clip is from Alas Kedaton Monkey Forest , where I filmed huge fruit bats hanging among the trees. They are flying foxes from the Pteropus group, which includes some of the world’s largest bats . Seeing them gathered in the forest was a very different wildlife moment from visiting the monkeys in Ubud. Your browser does not support this video. Alas Kedaton · Bali Big bats in the forest canopy. The flying foxes are an unforgettable part of this wildlife stop. Their size makes the name feel fitting when you see them hanging in the trees. The honest postcard Beautiful memories, difficult realities. I want to be honest: I have some regret about choosing to live on Bali for three months. It is not because of the people I met, the culture I got to know or the fun I had. It is because the island felt far too crowded for me. Traffic could turn a five-kilometre ride into an hour on the road. The beaches on Bali itself were not always as beautiful as the ones I had seen online; the nearby islands offered the clearer water and scenery I had imagined. I also noticed litter across public areas, plastic being burned, and air that felt heavily polluted. After more than fifteen minutes on a scooter, I could sometimes run a fingernail over my skin and see a dark mark. That made the pollution feel very real to me. These are my impressions from the places I visited, and one of the reasons I do not expect to return to Bali soon. Bali gave me days I would relive in a heartbeat—and a few realities I could not edit out of the frame. What I carry with me If I could go back to see the people I met and share those experiences with my family again, I would be there in a heartbeat. For a longer stay, though, the crowds, traffic and pollution changed how I felt about the island. Thailand still has my heart as my favourite place in the region. title: Philippines Travel Story: Beneath the Philippine Blue
text: My 2025 Philippines adventure with friends: Oslob, Bohol, Boracay, El Nido and Manila, with personal films, photographs and fascinating island facts.
keywords: Home Travel stories Philippines Philippines · 2025 · Travelling with friends Beneath the Philippine blue. Island roads, late nights and a change of plans. The trip I had waited for gave me far more than a beautiful view. Words, photographs & films by Dainyel August–September 2025 Island hopping Approx. 17 min read Read at your own pace. Explore the chapters below. El Nido · A view worth looking back on. Watch the full flight ↗ At a glance A 2025 adventure with friends: Cebu, Oslob, Bohol, Boracay, El Nido and Manila. Island roads, late nights and an unexpected change of plans. Explore this destination → · Small moments from the archive → In this story Cebu & the beginning Oslob & Tumalog Panglao & Bohol Boracay El Nido A change of plans Manila What stayed with me Back to the opening ↑ The beginning · Cebu City The bucket-list trip, finally. Here it is: the Philippines. After my earlier adventures in Southeast Asia, this was the country sitting right at the top of my list. Why? Honestly, I did not have a very good answer. I had a picture of it in my head, but almost no idea what being there would actually feel like. Then I arrived. Wow. I had just been travelling alone in Thailand , so my journey began with a flight from Chiang Mai to Manila and another to Cebu City. This time, I would be exploring with friends. Different energy, different stories, and a lot less peace and quiet. Looking back, it became one of the biggest adventures I have had—and one I remember with a ridiculous amount of happiness. But first: getting everyone together. I reached our hotel about three hours before the rest of the group arrived. A few of the boys were already in Cebu and had done some exploring. The city? Well… mostly its nightlife. Conveniently, that meant they already knew where to take us for dinner and a drink. Those first days were more about eating, bars and laughing at each other than serious sightseeing. Cebu is a big city, but for our trip it worked best as a starting point. We were ready to get to the islands. After three nights out, though, we had already gathered enough stories for a film. Think The Hangover , Cebu edition. What happens in the Philippines stays in the Philippines. Some of it, anyway. Did you know? · The bigger picture 7,641 islands. One very small sample. The Philippines is an archipelago of 7,641 islands, grouped into Luzon, the Visayas and Mindanao. Our journey only scratched the surface. Source: Philippine Embassy in The Hague ↗ How our trip unfolded Cebu → Oslob → Panglao/Bohol → Cebu → Boracay, via Malay → El Nido → Puerto Princesa → Manila. We took the bus south to Oslob, boats to Panglao and back to Cebu, then flights towards Boracay and El Nido. After El Nido, a public bus took us to Puerto Princesa for our flight to Manila. Oslob · South along Cebu An early alarm. A very big fish. The bus to Oslob was supposed to take around five hours. Supposed to. Seven or eight hours later, we finally arrived, and a long bus ride does not become more enjoyable with a hangover. Our hostel was a welcome landing: friendly people, a game of pool, some conversation and an evening to recover. We needed the rest. Our alarm went off at 5:30 the next morning because we were going swimming with whale sharks. Yes, whale sharks. I had no idea what to expect, but an enormous crowd at six in the morning was not it. It felt like a thousand or two thousand people were already waiting. The crowd was much bigger than I had imagined. Had I known how touristy it would be, I would have thought harder about joining. We went ahead, and the size of the animals was unbelievable. They swam right beside us, close enough that I felt one brush against me. It was one of those moments when your brain needs a second to catch up with what is happening. Did you know? · Beneath the surface Meet the world’s largest fish. It is the world’s largest fish and a filter feeder, eating tiny prey such as plankton and fish eggs. Researchers can also recognise individual whale sharks by their spot patterns. NOAA Fisheries ↗ · LAMAVE research ↗ A little context for this memory Oslob’s encounters involve feeding, which LAMAVE’s research links to changes in whale shark behaviour . The encounter rules prohibit touching or riding the animals. The contact I remember is not something to seek out: give wildlife space, never chase it, and read about the encounter guidelines before deciding whether a tour fits the way you want to travel. Your browser does not support this video. Oslob · Beneath the Philippine blue The whale shark moment from the original story preview. Open the film directly . And that was only the beginning of the day. Our guide took us to Tumalog Falls , where the water felt freezing. Outside, it was around 35 degrees; in the pool, I suddenly had rather less to say about the heat. Brrr. The huge curtain of water, the green surroundings and all of us together made it another day I will not forget. There was barely time to stop. Once the tour finished, we were off to the boat for the next island. Dry off, pack up, move on. We were really doing this. Oslob · The village and hills from above Tumalog Falls · Cold water on a hot day Tumalog Falls · One for the group album Panglao & Bohol · Taking the long way The road was half the adventure. Our next base was Panglao, in Bohol province. We rented scooters on arrival and headed to Glamping Alona . In practice, we mostly slept there. The days were for exploring, and in the evenings we ended up playing pool at Escape Alona Beach Bar . A new island, a familiar routine. One thing I want to be clear about: being able to rent a scooter easily does not mean you are allowed or insured to ride it. Many vehicles sold as “scooters” are motorcycles. Check the vehicle category, your licence, any International Driving Permit or translation requirements, and the terms of your insurance before renting. Our group had riding experience, but experience does not replace the right licence. NetherlandsWorldwide explains what an IDP does ; check the Philippines-specific licence information too. The next early start took us towards the Chocolate Hills . Our scooter journey took about four hours, and I would happily relive the scenery along that ride. Quiet stretches of road, green countryside, villages and little glimpses of everyday life: getting there became a huge part of the memory. There was also a moment of perspective. Coming from Europe, I realised how comfortable my own life was. At the same time, I found myself wondering what I would give up to live somewhere surrounded by this much nature. I was seeing it as a visitor, of course, with a very different set of worries from someone making a life there. Still, the thought stayed with me. Did you know? · Getting your bearings Panglao: an island within Bohol province. Panglao is an island in Bohol province, connected by bridges to the larger island of Bohol. Staying near Alona Beach puts you on Panglao; the Chocolate Hills are inland on Bohol. Source: Bohol Provincial Tourism Office ↗ And the hills themselves? A landscape that almost looks invented: rounded mounds rolling away into the distance. Add the Bilar man-made forest and the roads between the stops, and it was a lot more than one viewpoint. I loved that whole day. Chocolate Hills · A view that almost looks invented Bohol · Looking out across the Chocolate Hills Chocolate Hills · A little context behind the view Bilar man-made forest · The journey between the stops Did you know? · Why “chocolate”? The colour changes with the season. The UNESCO Tentative List description records about 1,776 Chocolate Hills. Their grassy covering turns brown in the dry season, giving them their name. The hills are natural limestone formations shaped by erosion. Source: UNESCO World Heritage Centre ↗ Bohol · From above The hills beyond the viewpoint. Watch the full flight ↗ Did you know? · Beyond the viewpoint Bohol became the Philippines’ first UNESCO Global Geopark. The designation came in 2023. The Chocolate Hills are part of its wider geological story, with limestone formed from ancient coral reefs. The roadside mahogany forest around Bilar and Loboc is different: a planted forest stretching for about two kilometres. UNESCO Global Geoparks ↗ · Bohol Tourism ↗ But our next connection was waiting, so eventually we had to leave. The boat took us back to… Cebu City. We had missed it so much that we simply had to return. All right, not quite. Going through Cebu made sense for our route. And since we were there, we might as well surprise the people at the bars again. The next day, we were heading for what felt like paradise. There was just one small obstacle: a propeller plane. My favourite. And by favourite, I mean one of my biggest fears. Spoiler: I survived. Boracay · Five days by the water A roof terrace, a seafood feast, a sunset. After travelling via Malay, we reached Boracay by boat and took a little tricycle from the harbour. My first impression changed as we moved across the island. Everyday streets gave way to the busy beach side, and suddenly there it was: white sand, incredibly blue water, greenery and small boats scattered across the sea. Touristy? Absolutely. Beautiful? Also absolutely. We stayed five days at Mayuma Beach Villa . There were eight of us there, spread across three floors with bedrooms, living spaces, bathrooms and kitchens. It felt enormous for our group. Two members of staff helped us during the stay, and then there was the roof terrace. Honestly, that terrace deserves its own paragraph. We watched sunsets from up there, with boats out on the water and the light changing over the beach. Those are the evenings I remember very clearly. The later nights? Some are a little less sharp. The clubs were around a twenty-minute walk from our villa, and we made good use of that. We ate out together, but some of our best meals started at the market. We bought seafood—huge prawns, oysters, fish and other shellfish—and turned it into our own meal with several courses. A group of friends, a kitchen and far too much enthusiasm: it was a very good combination. Did you know? · That long strip of white White Beach stretches for around four kilometres. Boracay sits just off the northwestern tip of Panay. White Beach faces west, while Bulabog Beach is on the island’s eastern side—two quite different coastal settings on one small island. Source: Philippine Department of Tourism ↗ Boracay · White Beach from above Boracay · The coastline stretching into the distance Boracay · A little beach-side welcome Boracay · Evening light from above the beach Boracay · Boats in the evening light Boracay · A sunset worth staying for Boracay · A small encounter beneath the surface Boracay · A different world below the boat Boracay · Travel films The coast, our roof terrace and a morning at the seafood market. Your browser does not support this video. Boracay · Along the coast 0:36 · My footage from the trip. Open the film directly . Your browser does not support this video. Boracay · From our roof terrace to sunset 0:08 · My footage from the trip. Open the film directly . Your browser does not support this video. Boracay · Choosing seafood at the market 0:12 · My footage from the trip. Open the film directly . A beach seller also talked us into an island tour. We snorkelled, jumped from cliffs and visited beaches we would probably never have reached on our own. It was genuinely a lot of fun. There is something special about going out on a boat and seeing the coast from another angle, rather than always looking towards the water from the shore. Eventually, the Boracay chapter had to end. The adventure, fortunately, did not. Another flight, another propeller plane, another opportunity for me to pretend I was completely relaxed. Next stop: El Nido. El Nido · Above the coast, between the islands The kind of blue you keep trying to photograph. In El Nido we rented another villa, a little smaller this time, and hired scooters again. We had hardly settled into this new chapter before we were off to the El Nido Zipline . Doing that together, with the sea and islands below, was exactly the sort of activity that made this trip feel like an adventure. In the evenings, we went to Amigos . The nightlife was another part of El Nido for us, alongside the views and excursions. Somehow, we kept finding enough energy for both. Then came our island-hopping day: Tour A. We visited beautiful places, went kayaking and spent a lot of time laughing. I also had the chance to fly my drone. Getting those shots was exciting, but sending it out over that landscape made me nervous too. The photographs and films bring back both feelings: the view in front of me and the concentration behind the camera. What I loved was the change of scale. From the boat, the cliffs looked huge. From a kayak, the water felt close and everything slowed down. From above, the beaches and boats became tiny details in a much bigger landscape. I could point a camera in almost any direction and still feel as if it was not quite capturing what being there was like. Did you know? · A living landscape El Nido’s scenery is part of a protected area. The El Nido Managed Resource Protected Area includes much more than dramatic rock: its ecosystems include forests, caves, coral reefs, seagrass and mangroves. The landscape above the water is only part of the picture. Source: DENR Biodiversity Management Bureau ↗ El Nido · The islands across the bay El Nido · Out between the islands El Nido · Green cliffs, bright water El Nido · A beach tucked beneath the cliffs El Nido · The bigger picture from above El Nido · Another view along the road El Nido · The everyday streets between adventures El Nido · A stop among the market stalls El Nido Zipline · Before the ride El Nido Zipline · Looking down towards the sea El Nido · A stop on our island tour El Nido · Getting closer to the water El Nido · The view from my kayak El Nido · A slower way to see the islands El Nido · Travel films A zipline ride, the islands from above and a moment in the kayak. Your browser does not support this video. El Nido Zipline · Come along for the ride 1:12 · My footage from the trip. Open the film directly . Your browser does not support this video. El Nido · From above The 28-second tour film already shared here. Open the film directly . Your browser does not support this video. El Nido · From the kayak 0:25 · My footage from the trip. Open the film directly . El Nido · When the plan stopped working You can plan a route. You cannot plan the weather. Then a typhoon crossed the Philippines, and our plans changed. We had wanted to continue to Moalboal and a few other islands, but instead we were stuck in El Nido. The mood was not always brilliant. After so many days of moving and doing things, suddenly being unable to continue was frustrating. I still tried to find something to enjoy. My best friend and I did a climbing course, and I went out on my own one evening. The canopy walk, the bay under low cloud and those wet, green views became another side of the trip. This is how that chapter unfolded for us; weather warnings and local closures should always decide which activities are possible. Eventually, we changed the route and aimed for Manila for the final part of the holiday. We took a public bus from El Nido to Puerto Princesa and flew from there. It was not the ending we had planned, but the trip was still giving us new experiences. They just looked rather different from the ones on our original list. Did you know? · Island weather A storm can change more than one day’s plans. PAGASA reports an average of about 20 tropical cyclones entering the Philippine Area of Responsibility each year; around eight or nine cross the Philippines. The area of responsibility is much larger than the country, so those figures do not mean 20 landfalls. July to October is the peak season. Source: PAGASA ↗ El Nido · Along the canopy walkway El Nido · A canopy walk with my best friend El Nido · The bay beneath low cloud El Nido · The view from the climbing course El Nido · A night out with friends Manila · One last change of scene From limestone cliffs to the concrete jungle. After the islands, Manila felt like stepping into another world. We had swapped all that nature for the concrete jungle. We went to a boxing show featuring performers of short stature, spent evenings out together and took things fairly slowly during the day. I also finally got the chest tattoo I had wanted for a long time. A souvenir that was definitely not going in my suitcase. I love travelling with a group, but I also need small breaks from all the noise and activity. That does not mean I am not enjoying myself. Sometimes, a few hours walking around alone are enough to feel like myself again. In Manila, I made room for those little escapes and some sightseeing, including the gate of Fort Santiago . Those walks gave me a different way to remember the city: church courtyards, street food, old trees and everyday scenes between the bigger sights. After so much time together, it was good to notice things at my own pace, then meet the others again with a little more energy. Did you know? · Behind the gate Fort Santiago has been rebuilt more than once. The Spanish fort dates to 1571, with its stone form built between 1589 and 1592. Its gate was destroyed during the Second World War and restored in the 1980s. The fort also held José Rizal as a prisoner before his execution. Intramuros: the gate ↗ · Museo ni Rizal ↗ Manila · A courtyard away from the traffic Manila · A quiet church interior Manila · Finding a quieter corner Manila · Small details along the street Manila · Everyday food on the street Manila · One of our last evenings out Looking back · The part you take home Beautiful, busy, and completely unforgettable. Then it was time for the Netherlands again. The flight home took around fifteen hours, and I think I slept through thirteen of them. After that trip, apparently even I had finally run out of energy. There is one part I have not said much about yet: the food. Normally, I am the person who wants to try local dishes, and you will not often find me choosing a fast-food chain. The Philippines somehow saw rather more of that version of me. KFC, McDonald’s, Burger King, Jollibee… there were plenty of choices, and we did not exactly make our healthiest decisions. I did try local food too. Some of the dishes I ate had sweeter flavours than I expected—especially coming straight from Thailand. I am not saying every Filipino dish tastes sweet, or that our choices represented the whole country’s cooking. It was simply a different flavour profile from the one I had just got used to, and I preferred some meals more than others. The market seafood we cooked together was its own very happy chapter. Did you know? · A familiar red sign Jollibee’s story started with ice cream. The family business began selling ice cream in Manila in 1975. Three years later, it moved towards hot meals and the Jollibee brand. One of the fast-food names we kept seeing had a very local beginning. Source: Jollibee Group’s history ↗ What stayed with me most was the welcome. We met friendly, hospitable people all along the way, and being able to communicate easily in English helped us connect. The landscapes were extraordinary, but it was the combination of people, nature, activities and time with friends that made the trip so special. Did you know? · A multilingual country Filipino and English are official languages. Filipino developed from a Tagalog base. Alongside Filipino and English, the constitution recognises regional languages as auxiliary official languages in their regions—a small reminder that one country can hold many different voices. 1987 Constitution, Article XIV ↗ · 1937 national-language order ↗ What stayed with me I went to the Philippines with a bucket-list idea and came home with a very real collection of memories: a bus journey that would not end, freezing waterfall water, long island roads, rooftop sunsets, nervous flights and a lot of laughter. It was beautiful, busy and occasionally frustrating. It was also an adventure I am incredibly glad we shared. Some trips give you the view you imagined. This one gave me a story I could never have planned. Have a question about travelling through the Philippines with friends? Ask me about the Philippines → Keep the curiosity going Another place. Read Brevo’s privacy policy ↗ and Google’s privacy policy ↗ for their processing and international transfer information. The form and its CAPTCHA load when you open the sign-up form. Community challenges Challenge suggestions and optional nicknames remain private until the owner approves them. Edits return to review. Keep the private edit key to change your own suggestion; the key is not included in public content. Necessary abuse protection uses Firebase App Check and short-lived, hashed rate-limit identifiers. No visitor GPS is collected. How long information is kept Unpublished questions and replies: up to 90 days after submission for review. Rejected submissions are removed when no longer needed for moderation. These are reviewed at least annually; there is no fixed expiry for the public story archive. Newsletter and earlier Field Notes registrations: up to 24 months after registration, or sooner if you withdraw or the updates service ends. After unsubscribing, only the minimum record needed to honour your opt-out is retained; it is not used to send updates. Privacy requests: only for resolving the request and documenting its outcome, for up to 12 months after closure, unless a specific legal obligation or dispute requires longer retention. Website records are reviewed and removed manually by the owner; there is no automatic deletion job. Google controls the retention of its service security logs separately. For example, Firebase Hosting retains request IP data for a few months, as described in Firebase’s privacy information ↗ . Website hosting, database and security Google Firebase provides hosting, Firestore, owner authentication and abuse protection. Network and browser details, including IP addresses and security tokens, may be processed to deliver the site, prevent spam and protect access. I rely on the legitimate interest of operating a secure, reliable website (Article 6(1)(f) GDPR) for necessary security processing. You can object through the contact channel above. Only the authorised owner can manage private submissions and registrations. Google processes service data under its applicable terms. Optional website analytics With your permission, Google Analytics measures visits and page usage to help improve this website. Advertising and its consent service are off for now, so Analytics does not depend on AdSense approval. Rejecting does not prevent reading stories or signing up. The legal basis is your consent (Article 6(1)(a) GDPR). Newsletter addresses, question text and account details are not sent as custom analytics events. Configured page locations exclude query strings and arbitrary fragments. Known public panels such as the atlas, Q&A and films use fixed names so their visits can be counted separately. Search text and unknown error-page paths are not sent. Google signals and advertising personalisation features within Google Analytics remain disabled. Your Analytics-only choice is saved in this browser for up to 180 days. An expired, invalid or missing record asks again. Change or withdraw your choice on the Cookies & settings page . Withdrawing stops subsequent measurement, clears this site's Analytics cookies and reloads the page; it does not remove records already sent. Analytics cookies have a configured lifetime of up to six months. Contact support@dainyelonthemove.com about earlier data. The Analytics account is configured to retain event-level data for two months and user-level data for fourteen months. The user-level retention period resets on new activity. These controls do not determine the retention of most aggregated standard reports. Read Google's privacy policy . Advertising is off for now The website retains the public AdSense ownership metadata and ads.txt authorisation while the advertising setup is reviewed. Those records do not load advertisements or Google’s advertising consent service. The current Analytics permission is not advertising consent. If advertising is launched later, the certified Google consent message will replace the Analytics-only message and ask for the relevant choices; previous Analytics-only acceptance will not automatically grant advertising permission. The homepage journey and Postcards reminders save only local dismissal preferences to avoid repeatedly interrupting your visit. These preferences do not check, reveal or change your newsletter subscription or social-media following. External social links contact the relevant platform only when you choose to open them. Read the cookie and player notice . Videos, Instagram and other external services Videos hosted with this website do not load a social platform. An external player connects only after you choose to load it. External platforms then process technical information and may use cookies under their own policies. Following an external link also takes you to that provider. See the cookie and player notice . The contact form stores your name, reply email, chosen topic, message and any optional project details privately in Firebase. A background service using GitHub Actions and Brevo delivers the enquiry to Dainyel’s fixed owner mailbox after production activation; the test website saves messages only in a separate private test inbox and sends no contact mail. The form clearly reports if the service is unavailable. Enquiries are used to reply, not to subscribe you to marketing. Your choices and rights You can request access, correction or deletion of your information, withdraw consent, request restriction or portability where applicable, or object to processing based on legitimate interests. Email Dainyel at support@dainyelonthemove.com. Requests are normally answered within one month; if a lawful extension is needed, you will be told why. You can also complain to the Dutch Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens ↗ , or your local data protection authority. title: Thailand Study Exchange: Three Months
text: A personal story about three months in Thailand: studying in Nonthaburi, Bangkok, Khao Sok, islands, wildlife and new perspectives.
keywords: Home Travel stories Thailand study exchange Thailand · 2024 · study exchange Thailand: the land of smiles… Three months of new flavours, city streets, quiet water and a wider view of the world. Words & images by Dainyel August 2024 3 months Study exchange Approx. 7 min read Read at your own pace. Explore the chapters below. A quieter side of Thailand · Khao Sok My exchange gave me the time to do more than pass through. I could get to know a different culture, meet people with their own ways of seeing the world, and reflect on what I thought I already knew. For me, a trip is not a checklist of places or a measure of what you spend. It is the perspective you take home—and the little moments that stay with you. Exchange chapter · Southeast Asia Thailand, the land of smiles… At least, that is what they said. In August 2024, I left the Netherlands for my first big journey into Asia. I was excited, of course, but a little nervous too. It would be my first time away from home for more than five months, with three of them spent discovering Thailand as part of my International Business degree. At a glance Three months of new flavours, city streets, quiet water and a wider view of the world. Explore this destination → · Small moments from the archive → In this story Travel notebook Bangkok & food Pattaya & nights Khao Sok Islands & history Wildlife Back to the opening ↑ From my 2024 Polarsteps journal One home base. So many changes of scene. Nonthaburi became my everyday base. Between classes, the journey stretched from Bangkok and Pattaya to the islands and the jungle. These are a few of the moments I wrote down along the way. Late August Settling into Pak Kret A first campus tour, street-food stalls and a new routine just north of Bangkok. September Bangkok & Ancient City Temple visits, the skyline from above and a golf cart through Ancient City. Late September Phuket & Patong A flight south, a couple of days exploring and then a bus towards Khao Sok. Late September Four days in Khao Sok River tubing, a night walk, kayaking and one night sleeping on the lake. Early October Across to Phi Phi A boat from Phuket, new people and a walk up to the island viewpoint. The final week A family visit My parents came to Thailand before it was time for me to move on. A classroom with a local connection Studying in Nonthaburi My home base was Nonthaburi, just north of Bangkok, where I took an exchange minor in Integrated Digital Marketing at Panyapiwat Institute of Management (PIM) . One fun link between campus and everyday life: PIM was founded under CP ALL , the company that operates 7-Eleven stores in Thailand . Those familiar signs were everywhere, so the connection between my studies and the world around me was hard to miss. Nonthaburi My study base Integrated Digital Marketing Exchange minor In my first Polarsteps entry from Pak Kret, I was still adjusting to the heat. Our first Monday brought an introduction and a tour of campus. Outside class, the street-food stalls and familiar 7-Eleven signs were quickly becoming part of everyday life. Bangkok · A city of flavours Follow the streets, follow your appetite. Bangkok made a big first impression. In Chinatown, the colour and energy of the streets pulled me towards the food stalls. I tried fresh local dishes, along with some more unusual bites—including insects. There was always something new to look at, smell or taste. I remember some meals costing around 37 to 80 baht—roughly one or two euros at the time. That felt incredibly affordable from my European point of view. But a low price for a visitor can still be a meaningful amount for someone who lives and works locally. It made me think twice about calling a place “cheap” as if everyone experiences its prices in the same way. One September entry took me from temple visits to the view from MahaNakhon. Another brought Ancient City: a huge park to explore, and I happily chose a golf cart. Bangkok kept giving me a different way to spend a day. Finding my way through Chinatown A market full of choices An adventurous market bite Everyday Thai food A new flavour around every corner Chinatown, after dark Bangkok from above · MahaNakhon A quieter moment at Wat Pho Ancient City · an afternoon exploring by golf cart City nights · Pattaya More than one side to a night out. I got to know Bangkok’s nightlife, and weekend trips to Pattaya brought a different change of pace: evenings out, visits to animal parks and time to explore the city’s landmarks. The intricately carved Sanctuary of Truth stood out for its scale and detailed wooden architecture. Back in Bangkok, seeing Wat Arun glowing beside the river after dark gave the city another mood altogether. Sanctuary of Truth · Pattaya Wat Arun after dark A Chinatown street memory The city lights from the river Khao Sok · A change of rhythm The best connection was being present. If Bangkok was constant motion, Khao Sok was the reset. My Polarsteps notes bring those four days back clearly: river tubing and a jungle walk on our first evening, then a boat out to the lake for an overnight stay. We went kayaking, walked to waterfalls and got up early for sunrise on the water. After the lake, we returned to the jungle for one more night and a long morning hike. The landscape alone was enough to slow me down. For roughly half our stay, there was no internet. I expected that to be inconvenient; instead, it felt like a gift. No steady stream of notifications, no doom-scrolling—just the people around me and the place we had come to experience. I remember how good it felt to be properly present. Sometimes the most memorable part of a trip is what you finally get to tune out. A memory from the lake Room to breathe. Calm water, forested hills and floating lodges made Khao Sok feel a world away from the city. The night walk added a little wildness too: you never quite know what you might spot in the trees. A quiet morning at the floating lodges A night-walk encounter On the way to our lake stay One night on the lake Late light on the lake A different world from Bangkok Back into the jungle Islands & history Thailand kept changing the view. Phuket was the starting point for this trip south. After four days in Khao Sok, we returned there for a night in a cabin hostel before taking the boat to Phi Phi. We met new people, spent time on the water and walked up to the lookout point. The sea and steep green islands gave us a completely different view. My phone even ended up in the water on a boat trip—a less welcome memory, but thankfully I still had everything. Inland, Ayutthaya offered another kind of perspective. It was once the capital of Siam and became a major centre of trade and diplomacy; today, its temple ruins make that history feel close enough to walk through. The city is recognised as a UNESCO World Heritage site . Phi Phi Islands Layers of history in Ayutthaya The day slowing down · Patong Beach A soft spot for animals Wildlife stops, wherever I go. I’m a big animal lover, so visiting a wildlife park or zoo is something I often try to make room for when I travel. Thailand gave me plenty of animal encounters to remember—from an elephant up close to a capybara visit and seeing the hippos that included Moo Deng. They added a playful, personal thread to a journey full of cities, landscapes and culture. An elephant encounter Meeting the capybaras A visit to see Moo Deng The last entry One more reason to come back. In my last week in Thailand, my parents came to visit me and see the country. By then, I was sad to be leaving. I ended my Polarsteps notes certain of one thing: this would not be my last time in Thailand. What stayed with me So, is Thailand the land of smiles? For me, it was also a place of contrasts: busy streets and quiet water, late nights and early adventures, new flavours and familiar routines seen in a new light. I arrived for an exchange and left with a wider view of the world—and a reminder that travel is less about ticking places off a map than learning to see through someone else’s perspective. Three months in Thailand gave me more than memories of where I went. It changed the way I look at the world. Have a question about my three-month exchange in Thailand? title: Solo Thailand: An Eight-Day Journey
text: Follow Dainyel’s first solo Thailand trip through Bangkok, Pattaya, Chiang Rai and Chiang Mai before meeting friends in the Philippines.
keywords: Home Travel stories Thailand solo Thailand · Solo journey · 2025 Thailand, on my own. Eight days, five stops and my first time setting off alone. It became one of the most personal trips I have taken. Words & images by Dainyel Thailand 2025 Solo trip Approx. 1 min read Read at your own pace. Explore the chapters below. A moment to pause · Thailand, 2025 A different Thailand chapter Going alone changed the way I travelled. This trip was not memorable because of one particular sight or one packed itinerary. It mattered because it was my first solo trip. I am naturally social and have never found it difficult to start a conversation, but booking that flight alone was still a different kind of step. Before joining my friends in the Philippines, I gave myself eight days in Thailand: Bangkok , Pattaya , Bangkok again, then Chiang Rai and Chiang Mai . I went alone, but the trip kept proving that solo travel does not have to mean being lonely. Eight days · one first solo trip Familiar places, a new kind of confidence. I already knew Thailand well enough to arrive with a few favourite places in mind. What I did not know was how much room a short solo journey could make for chance encounters, local conversations and doing things at exactly my own pace. At a glance Eight days, five stops and my first time setting off alone. Explore this destination → · Small moments from the archive → In this story Back to the opening ↑ A moment to pause There was time for the quieter side too. Between flights, scooters, night markets and late conversations, I still found moments that slowed the whole journey down. Sitting in a temple while monks gathered in front of the Buddha was one of them. It reminded me that Thailand can feel completely different depending on how you choose to move through it. The real adventure started when I stopped waiting for a plan and started following the day. Bangkok · A soft landing Starting alone, surrounded by familiar faces. I began in Bangkok with three nights in a hotel close to the centre. I was travelling on a budget, but after a long flight I wanted to give myself a comfortable start: a proper room, a pool and a little space to reset. On the first evening I unexpectedly ran into a good friend from the Netherlands who was travelling through Thailand with his girlfriend. Bangkok already felt a little less lonely. Because I knew the city from earlier trips, I spent my days wandering through familiar streets and finding corners I had missed before. In the evenings, another coincidence appeared: two more friends were also in Thailand, including a former roommate from my earlier months in Thailand and Bali. The plan had been to travel solo, yet the city gave me some of the people I knew best at exactly the right time. One night back in Bangkok, before heading north, I stayed in a hostel and finally felt completely on my own in the best way. I spent the day sightseeing, then headed to Chinatown for food. It was a small reset before the part of the trip where I knew nobody at all. Pattaya · Friends in familiar places A return that felt personal. In Pattaya, I visited a friend who had chosen to stay in Thailand after our minor. I checked into Harry’s Hotel , a place I already knew from my earlier time in the country. Over three months I had become friendly with the manager and staff, so coming back felt more like seeing people again than simply checking into a hotel. I also met two Dutch travellers who had unexpectedly crossed paths even though they already knew one another from home. The nights that followed were the kind people summarize with a smile: what happens in Thailand stays in Thailand. The best part was the reminder that travelling alone still leaves plenty of room for shared stories. Chiang Rai · A chance connection One small favour turned into a travel friendship. On the flight to Chiang Rai, I helped a French traveller with his backpack at the airport. The next day, I saw him again while exploring the city’s temples. It was such a random moment that we had to laugh. We spent time together around Wat Rong Khun , the White Temple, the Chiang Rai Clock Tower and Wat Rong Suea Ten , better known as the Blue Temple. We ate near the Blue Temple, exchanged contacts and later met again at the Chiang Rai Night Bazaar . The night was simple: food, a beer, pool and the local way of going out. It was proof that one friendly moment can change an entire stop on a journey. Chiang Mai · Following my own pace Choosing local moments over the obvious plan. I finished in Chiang Mai at Mad Monkey . Even in a party hostel, I was more interested in finding the local rhythm than joining every group plan. A rented scooter gave me the freedom to head out during the day and see places including Wat Phra Singh , Wat Chedi Luang , Wat Phra That Doi Suthep and Baan Tong Luang . The moment that stayed with me most came at Lanna Elephant Care . After a long scooter ride I arrived near closing time and thought I had missed my chance. Instead, after a long conversation with one of the caretakers, he arranged a small private visit. I could walk beside the elephants, feed them, help with their bath and simply spend time around them. Later, he even took me for food at a local roadside spot. That generosity was as memorable as the elephants themselves. If you do not try, you never know. I met the French traveller again in Chiang Mai too, and our conversations continued over drinks and pool. Along the way I met many more people, swapped contacts and made connections I might cross paths with again somewhere else in the world. That is one of the things I love most about travel: the map gets bigger, but so does your circle. What this trip gave me Flying solo did not mean doing everything alone. It meant deciding where to go next, saying yes to conversations and trusting that the unfamiliar would work itself out. Eight days later, I flew from Chiang Mai to meet my friends in the Philippines with more confidence than I had when I arrived. Want to read about my earlier time in Thailand?
